headline: US long-end yields at decade highs reflect a structural shift: the US must now compete for a shrinking pool of global capital rather than enjoy a free lunch on its deficit
reasoning: Brown argues the rise in US yields is both cyclical and structural. On the structural side, the US deficit and debt pile are so large that investors are questioning why the US deserves the premium safe-haven status that once let it borrow at exceptionally low rates. The Asian savings glut that recycled Chinese and Japanese capital into US Treasuries is unwinding — China faces demographic headwinds and Japan's own yields have risen sharply from near zero, pulling Japanese capital home. As a result, the US government must now compete with high-quality corporate borrowers (such as Alphabet) for a limited pool of global savings, and the only way to do that is to offer higher yields. The US 30-year hit decade-long highs and the Australian 10-year hit a 15-year high.
quote: The the the amount of capital in the world is. It's no longer sloshing around the world the same way that it used to across the 1990s and the 2000. People used to talk about the Asian savings glut, which was that China and Japan were sending huge amounts of capital out into the world, and that was being used by countries like the US to run large deficits and accrue large stocks of debt. Now, obviously in China, the the demographic changes have flown through have flowed through. And you're saying to see a different structure now they're they're pulling some of their capital back. Japan. The US 30 year yields in Japan have risen dramatically. They used to be around zero. They're now not far below other countries yields. So a lot of Japanese capital which used to go out to the rest of the world seeking higher yields, is now being pulled back home. And so it's not that the US is untrustworthy. This is they have to compete and sort of demonstrate why they are the appropriate home for your savings. And the only way they can do that is with higher yields.

headline: Private credit failures are a genuine crack, not idiosyncratic — high double-digit returns always carried meaningful risk now coming to the fore

He frames this as a return to rationality: investors should expect some strong years and some medium-sized loss years in private credit.
quote: Private credit managed to do very well for a period because these idiosyncratic risks never really didn't come to the fore. Over the last few years. And I think this is a bit more of a return to rationality, where people understand that, yes, you can achieve 10 or 12% in private credit, and every so often you'll get a large loss. It's not quite the misunderstanding was people thinking that private credit wasn't risky. It is a risky form of investment and you will make some really good returns some years, and you will have some medium sized losses in other years.
